[[Reactionary|Reactionarism]]}} | position = [[Far-right politics|Far-right]]{{cite news|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/christchurch-shooting/113929249/populist-and-farright-rhetoric-gains-currency-in-new-zealands-political-fringe|title=Populist and far-right rhetoric gains currency in New Zealand's political fringe|publisher=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |first=Thomas|last=Manch|date=7 July 2019}}{{cite web|url=https://www.wsws.org/en/articles/2019/07/02/dest-j02.html|title=New Zealand media promote new far-right Christian party|publisher=World Socialist Web Site|first=Tom|last=Peters|date=2 July 2019}} | religion = [[Destiny Church (New Zealand)|Destiny Church]] | headquarters = 44 Bob Charles Drive, [[Golflands]], [[Botany, New Zealand|Botany]], [[Auckland]] | website = [https://www.vision.org.nz/ vision.org.nz] }} '''Vision NZ''' is a [[Christian nationalism|nationalist]] political party in [[New Zealand]] led by [[Hannah Tamaki]], the co-leader of the [[fundamentalist Christian]] movement [[Destiny Church (New Zealand)|Destiny Church]].{{cite news|author=Jamie Ensor|date=23 May 2019|title=Hannah Tamaki to lead new political party Coalition New Zealand|work=[[Newshub]]|url=https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2019/05/brian-and-hannah-tamaki-to-lead-new-destiny-church-political-party.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190523031140/https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2019/05/brian-and-hannah-tamaki-to-lead-new-destiny-church-political-party.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=23 May 2019|access-date=23 May 2019|quote=On Thursday, Hannah was announced as the leader of the party, saying it is not a party just for Christians but for everyone who feels frustrated with the current Government. Brian promised the party would be a 'vehicle' for the 'silent majority' to express their beliefs.}}{{Cite web|title=Party profile: Vision NZ|url=https://policy.nz/parties/Vision-NZ|access-date=10 September 2020|website=Your complete guide to NZ Election 2020 — Policy|language=en-US|archive-date=26 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211026234214/https://policy.nz/parties/Vision-NZ|url-status=dead}}{{cite news |author=Melanie Earley |date=23 May 2019 |title=Destiny Church launches political party, promising 'politics with teeth' |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/112938679/destiny-church-launches-political-party-promising-politics-with-teeth |access-date=23 May 2019}} Its policies have included opposition to abortion, homosexuality, immigration, and the construction of new mosques. It has supported creating a Māori-owned bank and [[Ngāi Tūhoe|Tūhoe]] ownership of [[Te Urewera]], and has called for government funding for Destiny Church programmes. The party was announced in May 2019. It contested the [[2020 New Zealand general election]] both for electorate seats and the party-list vote, receiving 0.1% of the party vote and winning no seats. After the [[Freedoms New Zealand]] party formed in 2022, Vision NZ was registered as a component party of Freedoms NZ. At the [[2023 New Zealand general election|2023 election]], Freedoms NZ did not win any seats. == History == === Earlier parties associated with the Tamakis === {{see also|Destiny Church (New Zealand)|Destiny New Zealand}} Destiny Church was founded by [[Brian Tamaki]] in 1998{{Cite news|date=17 October 2017|title=14 things you might not know about Destiny Church|language=en-NZ|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11933787|access-date=10 September 2020|issn=1170-0777}} and is led by Brian and his wife Hannah Tamaki. Destiny New Zealand, a socially conservative Christian political party, was formed in 2003.{{Cite news|last=Taylor|first=Kevin|date=27 May 2003|title=Evangelist's church spawns Christian political party|language=en-NZ|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=3503680|access-date=10 September 2020|issn=1170-0777}} The party contested the [[2005 New Zealand general election]]; it received just over 14,000 party votes, or 0.62%, and won no seats.{{cite web|title=Official Count Results – Overall Status|url=http://2005.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2005/partystatus.html|publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]]|access-date=6 September 2014|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307010525/http://2005.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2005/partystatus.html|archive-date=7 March 2016}} It was deregistered as a political party in 2007.{{cite web|publisher=[[Newstalk ZB]]|title=Destiny Church widening political scope|date=17 September 2007|url=http://www.newstalkzb.co.nz/newsdetail1.asp?storyID=124514|access-date=17 September 2007|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081015193402/http://www.newstalkzb.co.nz/newsdetail1.asp?storyID=124514|archive-date=15 October 2008}} The official founder and former leader of the Destiny Party, [[Richard Lewis (New Zealand politician)|Richard Lewis]], created [[the Family Party]] in 2007.{{Cite web|date=17 October 2007|title=Another Christian political party announced|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10470379|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121103040458/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10470379|archive-date=3 November 2012|access-date=10 September 2020|website=[[New Zealand Herald]] }} The Destiny Church supported the Family Party in the [[2008 New Zealand general election]]. It won no seats{{Cite web|title=Official Count Results – Overall Status|url=https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2008/partystatus.html|access-date=10 September 2020|website=electionresults.govt.nz}} and was deregistered in 2010.{{Cite web|title=Amendments to the Registers of Political Parties and Logos|url=http://www.elections.org.nz/study/news/amendments-to-the-registers-of-political-parties-and-logos.html|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100514032057/http://www.elections.org.nz/study/news/amendments-to-the-registers-of-political-parties-and-logos.html|archive-date=14 May 2010|access-date=10 September 2020}} === Creation and registration === On 23 May 2019, [[Hannah Tamaki|Hannah]] and Brian Tamaki announced the creation of a new party, at the time called Coalition New Zealand, with Hannah Tamaki to lead the party. She would not talk about policies at the announcement. Brian described the aim of the party to become a vehicle for the "silent majority" to express their beliefs. The party had not created a website, and in the days following the announcement, a number of other people registered relevant [[domain name]]s and social media handles to stymie the party.{{Cite news|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/entertainment/celebrities/113013185/chase-star-paul-sinha-takes-a-parting-swipe-at-brian-and-hannah-tamaki|title=Chase star Paul Sinha takes a parting swipe at Brian and Hannah Tamaki |date=27 May 2019 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]]|language=en|access-date=14 August 2019}}{{Cite news|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/112985518/kiwis-continue-to-troll-tamakis-coalition-party-snapping-up-domain-names|title=Kiwis continue to troll the Tamakis' Coalition Party, snapping up domain names |date=25 May 2019 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]]|language=en|access-date=14 August 2019}} On 10 July 2019 the party applied to the Electoral Commission for registration.{{cite web |url=https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2019/application-to-register-coalition-new-zealand-party-and-logo/ |title=Application to register Coalition New Zealand party and logo |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|New Zealand Electoral Commission]] |date=10 July 2019 |access-date=16 July 2019}} On 16 August the Electoral Commission refused registration on the grounds that the party's name and logo was likely to mislead voters.{{cite news|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/115063129/electoral-commission-refuses-to-register-destiny-churchderived-party|title=Electoral Commission refuses to register Destiny Church-derived party, Coalition NZ|first=Kendall |last=Hutt |date=16 August 2019|work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]]|access-date=16 August 2019}}{{cite news|url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=12259211|title=Hannah Tamaki's Coalition NZ Party denied party registration|date=16 August 2019|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|access-date=16 August 2019}} In October 2019, the party announced a new name, Vision NZ, and a new logo, and applied to the Electoral Commission for registration again.{{Cite news|url=https://www-fusion.nzherald.co.nz/nz/destiny-churchs-hannah-tamaki-registers-new-political-party-name-vision-nz/HAEJB2C3E5CM3T7OQKTZLBVGD4/|title=Destiny Church's Hannah Tamaki registers new political party name Vision NZ|last=Walls|first=Jason|date=2 October 2019|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|access-date=1 October 2019|language=en-NZ|issn=1170-0777|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200309035833/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12272816|archive-date=9 March 2020|url-status=live}} The registration was confirmed on 4 December.{{cite web |url=https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2019/registration-of-political-parties-and-logos/ |title=Registration of political parties and logos |publisher=Electoral Commission |date=4 December 2019 |access-date=4 December 2019}} The party received a broadcasting allocation of $51,821 for the [[2020 New Zealand general election|2020 election]].{{cite web |url=https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2020/2020-broadcasting-allocation-decision-released/ |title=2020 Broadcasting Allocation Decision Released |publisher=Electoral Commission |date=29 May 2020 |access-date=29 May 2020}} === ''Dancing with the Stars'' and related events === In February 2020, Hannah Tamaki was understood to be a contestant on the upcoming ''[[Dancing with the Stars (New Zealand TV series)|Dancing with the Stars]]'' television show.{{Cite web|url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/410247/dancing-with-the-stars-could-wrong-foot-aspiring-politician-hannah-tamaki|title='Dancing with the Stars' could wrong-foot aspiring politician Hannah Tamaki|date=24 February 2020|website=[[RNZ]] |language=en-nz|access-date=24 February 2020}} Later that month, media company [[MediaWorks New Zealand]] announced that while Tamaki was originally going to be on the show, it had changed its mind and formally announced she was not to be in the show. A MediaWorks speaker said that "we have seen a very strong reaction, some of which has been extreme and concerning and MediaWorks does not condone bullying. We would be failing in our duty of care to everyone if we continued as planned."{{Cite web|url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/410316/mediaworks-confirms-hannah-tamaki-will-not-be-on-dancing-with-the-stars|title=Mediaworks confirms Hannah Tamaki will not be on Dancing with the Stars|date=25 February 2020|website=[[RNZ]] |language=en-nz|access-date=25 February 2020}} After a TV presenter commented on Tamaki's inclusion in ''Dancing with the Stars'', Vision NZ's campaign manager Jevan Goulter made a post on [[Facebook]] about the presenter. The post breached Facebook's community guidelines, media site [[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] declined to publish them, and {{As of|2020|February|lc=y}} police were assessing a complaint laid about the post. Tamaki fired Goulter for these comments.{{Cite web|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/entertainment/tv-radio/119790642/hannah-tamaki-sacks-campaign-manager-following-hate-speech-against-kanoa-lloyd|title=Hannah Tamaki sacks campaign manager following 'hate speech' against Kanoa Lloyd|last=Downes|first=Siobhan|date=25 February 2020|website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |language=en|access-date=25 February 2020}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/entertainment/tv-radio/119790642/hannah-tamaki-sacks-campaign-manager-following-hate-speech-against-kanoa-lloyd|title=Hannah Tamaki's campaign manager sacked as police consider social media complaint|last=Downes|first=Siobhan|date=25 February 2020|website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |language=en|access-date=25 February 2020}} Tamaki was asked by a journalist about similar comments by her husband Brian, who referred to "venomous, dirty liberal left, sexually confused antichrists", but Mrs Tamaki said she was not responsible for her husband's comments as they are not related to Vision NZ.{{Cite web|url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/checkpoint/audio/2018735752/hannah-tamaki-condemns-attack-post-but-dismisses-husband-brian-s-similar-post|title=Hannah Tamaki condemns attack post but dismisses husband Brian's similar post|last=Checkpoint|date=25 February 2020|website=[[RNZ]] |language=en-nz|access-date=25 February 2020}} === 2020 election campaign === By December 2019, the leaders of both major parties, [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour]] and [[New Zealand National Party|National]], had ruled out working with Vision NZ.{{Cite web|url=https://www.msn.com/en-nz/news/national/ardern-bridges-rule-out-working-with-hannah-tamakis-vision-nz/ar-AAK9IVP?li=BBqdg4K|title=Ardern, Bridges rule out working with Hannah Tamaki's Vision NZ|last=O'Brien|first=Tova|date=16 December 2019|website=MSN|access-date=24 February 2020}} In July 2020 it rejected a merger offer from the [[New Zealand Public Party]].{{cite web |url=https://www.waateanews.com/waateanews/x_news/MjUwMTc/Public-Party-praying-for-electoral-lifeline |title=Public Party praying for electoral lifeline |publisher=Waatea News |date=16 July 2020 |access-date=17 July 2020}} Vision submitted a [[Party-list proportional representation|party list]] of five people for the [[2020 New Zealand general election|2020 general election]], tied for the shortest list with the [[Heartland New Zealand Party|Heartland Party]].{{Cite web|title=Parties {{!}} Vote NZ|url=https://vote.nz/voting/get-ready-to-vote/parties/|access-date=19 September 2020|website=vote.nz|language=en-NZ|archive-date=21 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200921191449/https://www.vote.nz/voting/get-ready-to-vote/parties/|url-status=dead}} All five also [[Candidates in the 2020 New Zealand general election by electorate|contested electorates]], including Hannah Tamaki in the electorate of [[Waiariki (New Zealand electorate)|Waiariki]].{{cite web|date=17 June 2020|title=Vision NZ leader Hannah Tamaki to run for seat in general election|url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/419228/vision-nz-leader-hannah-tamaki-to-run-for-seat-in-general-election|access-date=19 June 2020|publisher=[[RNZ]] }}{{Cite web|title=Our Team|url=https://www.vision.org.nz/meet-our-team|access-date=10 September 2020|website=Vision New Zealand|language=en}} By September 2020, Vision NZ had only registered in one [[Colmar Brunton]] poll, receiving 0.1% of support in its May 2020 poll. In all other polls it had not registered any support.{{Cite web|date=21 May 2020|title=1 NEWS Colmar Brunton Poll: 16 – 20 May 2020|url=https://static.colmarbrunton.co.nz/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/Prelim_16-20-May-2020_1-NEWS-Colmar-Brunton-Poll-report-.pdf|page=6|access-date=1 October 2020|archive-date=21 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200921175839/https://static.colmarbrunton.co.nz/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/Prelim_16-20-May-2020_1-NEWS-Colmar-Brunton-Poll-report-.pdf|url-status=dead}}{{Cite web|date=28 September 2020|title=1 NEWS Colmar Brunton Poll: 23–27 September 2020|url=https://static.colmarbrunton.co.nz/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/PRELIM_23-27-September-2020_1-NEWS-Colmar-Brunton-Poll-report-.pdf|page=6}}{{Dead link|date=February 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }} An electorate poll for the [[Waiariki (New Zealand electorate)|Waiariki]] seat conducted in September 2020 showed that Vision NZ's leader, Hannah Tamaki, was only polling at 2%, compared to [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour]]'s [[Tāmati Coffey]] at 38% and the [[Māori Party]]'s [[Rawiri Waititi]] at 26%.{{Cite web|title=Undecided vote leaves Waiariki seat up for grabs|url=https://www.teaomaori.news/undecided-vote-leaves-waiariki-seat-grabs|access-date=4 October 2020|website=Maori TV}} Vision New Zealand received 4,236 party votes at the 2020 election, or 0.1%.{{cite web |date=6 November 2020 |title=2020 General Election and Referendums – Official Result |url=https://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/ |access-date=6 November 2020 |website=Electoral Commission}} Hannah Tamaki received 1,171 electorate votes in Waiariki (4% of the electorate vote), coming third behind [[Rawiri Waititi]] and [[Tāmati Coffey]].{{Cite web|date=6 November 2020|title=Waiariki – Official Result|url=https://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-72.html|access-date=6 November 2020|website=Electoral Commission}} Vision NZ won no seats, but Hannah Tamaki claimed after the election that her goal had always been to unseat Labour's candidate Coffey from the Waiariki electorate, and since that seat was won by Waititi, the party had achieved that goal.{{Cite web|last=Maxwell|first=Joel|date=28 October 2020|title=Election 2020: Good God! Destiny Church's Hannah Tamaki fulfills 'goal' to unseat Labour MP|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/123223342/election-2020-good-god-destiny-churchs-hannah-tamaki-fulfills-goal-to-unseat-labour-mp|access-date=28 October 2020|work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]]|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201102060935/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/123223342/election-2020-good-god-destiny-churchs-hannah-tamaki-fulfills-goal-to-unseat-labour-mp|archive-date=2 November 2020|url-status=live}} === Alliance with Freedoms New Zealand and 2023 campaign === During the [[COVID-19 protests in New Zealand#23 August|occupation of Parliament in August 2022]], Brian Tamaki announced the creation of a new political party, [[Freedoms New Zealand]].{{cite news |date=22 August 2022 |title=Brian Tamaki announces new political party |language=en-NZ |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/parliament-protest-brian-tamaki-announces-new-political-party-freedoms-nz/GYZSQDORMUKGO7MP3OMMAN2D6Q/ |access-date=24 August 2022}} Vision NZ was announced at the same time to be involved with the party, and Vision has since been officially registered as a component party of Freedoms NZ.{{Cite web |title=Register of political parties |url=https://elections.nz/democracy-in-nz/political-parties-in-new-zealand/register-of-political-parties/ |access-date=26 June 2023 |website=Elections |language=en-NZ}} On 31 May, Vision NZ, in conjunction with other parties associated with Freedoms NZ, sought a judicial review of the [[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]]'s broadcasting funding decision. The commission had allocated broadcasting funds to Freedoms NZ collectively rather than as individual political parties. Vision NZ and the other plaintiffs argued that the [[Broadcasting Act 1989]] did not clearly define what was a "group of parties" and that the Electoral Commission had not published a clear criteria for how their parties had joined forces.{{cite news |last1=Griffiths |first1=Ethan |date=31 May 2023 |title=Sue Grey and Brian Tamaki launch High Court action over election campaign funding |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/sue-grey-and-brian-tamaki-launch-high-court-action-over-election-campaign-funding/LNEGKH6G7FDNNEGI37ZPS65T3M/ |url-status=live |access-date=6 June 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230603190110/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/sue-grey-and-brian-tamaki-launch-high-court-action-over-election-campaign-funding/LNEGKH6G7FDNNEGI37ZPS65T3M/ |archive-date=3 June 2023}}{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=20 June 2023 |title=Minor parties sue over election broadcasting advertising funding |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/wellington/132361834/minor-parties-sue-over-election-broadcasting-advertising-funding |access-date=26 June 2023 |website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |language=en}} The New Zealand High Court dismissed the plaintiffs' claims.{{Cite web |last=The High Court of New Zealand |date=17 July 2023 |title=New Zealand Outdoors and Freedom Party v the Electoral Commission [2023] NZHC 1823 |url=https://www.courtsofnz.govt.nz/assets/cases/2023/MR-2023-NZHC-1823.pdf }}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} On 13 July 2023, Hannah Tamaki announced that Vision NZ would be contesting all seven [[Māori electorates]] during the [[2023 New Zealand general election]] as part of the Freedom NZ coalition. Tamaki stood as the party's candidate in the [[Tāmaki Makaurau (New Zealand electorate)|Tāmaki Makaurau]] electorate.{{cite news |last1=Los'e |first1=Joseph |title=It's Tamaki for Tamaki as Pastor Hannah stands in Auckland and reveals Vision NZ to contest seven Māori seats |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/its-tamaki-for-tamaki-as-pastor-hannah-stands-in-auckland-and-vision-nz-to-contest-all-7-maori-seats/CRHU2HNILFFUTBLAIM4QKDS2MU/ |access-date=29 September 2023 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=13 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230723154436/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/its-tamaki-for-tamaki-as-pastor-hannah-stands-in-auckland-and-vision-nz-to-contest-all-7-maori-seats/CRHU2HNILFFUTBLAIM4QKDS2MU/ |archive-date=23 July 2023|url-status=live}} Final results from the [[2023 New Zealand general election]] showed that Freedoms New Zealand received 0.33% of the party vote and did not win any electorate seats, meaning it will not enter parliament.{{cite web |title=2023 General Election – Official Result |url=https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/index.html |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]] |access-date=8 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231104213043/https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/index.html |archive-date=4 November 2023 |date=3 November 2023 |url-status=live}} Hannah Tamaki came last of five candidates in the [[Tāmaki Makaurau (New Zealand electorate)|Tāmaki Makaurau]] electorate, with 829 votes compared to the winning [[Te Pāti Māori]] candidate [[Takutai Tarsh Kemp]]'s 10,050 votes.{{cite web |title=Tāmaki Makaurau – Official Result |url=https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-68.html |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]] |access-date=8 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231108044925/https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-68.html |archive-date=8 November 2023 |date=3 November 2023 |url-status=live}} === Cuba St rainbow crossing controversy === In late 2024, Vision NZ party member [https://policy.nz/2023/rongotai-electorate/candidates/merania-deanna-roa Merania (Deanna) Roa] filed for filed a judicial review application in the High Court of New Zealand challenging the legality of a [[Cuba Street rainbow crossing|rainbow-coloured pedestrian crossing installed by Wellington City Council]].{{Cite web |date=2025-03-21 |title=Rainbow crossing legal case about safety, not diversity |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/legality-of-wellingtons-cuba-st-rainbow-crossing-challenged-in-the-high-court/BN7XSZ7ZGFDMJPPQHD54GF6XIQ/ |access-date=2025-03-21 |website=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |language=en-NZ}} In documents submitted to the court, Roa argued that the council’s decision to install the crossing was unlawful, claiming it was not a "prescribed traffic control device" under the Land Transport Rule: Traffic Control Devices 2004, and that the council had acted outside its powers under the Local Government Act 2002.{{Cite web |title=Roa v Wellington City Council [2025] NZHC 609 |url=https://www.courtsofnz.govt.nz/cases/roa-v-wellington-city-council- |access-date=2025-03-21 |website=Courts of New Zealand |language=en-GB}} In March 2025, the High Court dismissed the application, finding the council had acted lawfully and that the crossing did not pose a safety risk or contravene transport regulations. Costs were awarded against Roa and the other plaintiffs. The case attracted national media attention and drew widespread public criticism, with some claiming the action was "petty and ideologically motivated".{{Cite web |date=2025-03-21 |title=Here to stay: Court rules Wellington's rainbow crossing doesn't compromise safety |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/wellingtons-rainbow-crossing-to-stay-after-judical-review-dimissed/EXJYVLZ4ABDMJLFJ7TR7CGMMPI/ |access-date=2025-03-21 |website=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |language=en-NZ}} == Policies == Vision NZ has been described as a Christian party{{Cite web|last=Eleven|first=Beck|date=25 May 2019|title=I don't see Brian and Hannah Tamaki's Christian party lasting long|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/opinion/112993336/i-dont-see-this-new-attempt-at-a-christian-party-lasting-long|access-date=10 September 2020|website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |language=en}} and a "Destiny Church-derived party", but Hannah Tamaki has insisted that Vision NZ is not a Christian party, saying that "people don't have to go to church to be members of Vision New Zealand, they don't have to go to church to vote for Vision New Zealand."{{Cite news|last=Scotcher|first=Katie|date=10 September 2020|title=An introduction to 'The Outliers': The political parties who aren't in the daily headlines|url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/425718/an-introduction-to-the-outliers-the-political-parties-who-aren-t-in-the-daily-headlines|access-date=10 September 2020|work=[[Radio New Zealand]]|language=en-nz |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201214142354/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/425718/an-introduction-to-the-outliers-the-political-parties-who-aren-t-in-the-daily-headlines |archive-date=14 December 2020|url-status=live}} Vision opposes both abortion and homosexuality. Hannah Tamaki says that being gay is "wrong", though when discussing her opposition to gay MP [[Tāmati Coffey]] she said "If you do the work, I don’t care what you do, it’s your private life. I choose to live my Christian faith, and I don’t force that on anybody else." Brian Tamaki has said that homosexuality is a sin and has maintained there is a link between homosexuality and natural disasters. Hannah Tamaki has called for a ban on the construction of new mosques.{{cite news |title=Destiny Church's Hannah Tamaki calls for ban on new mosques |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12284163 |access-date=15 November 2019 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=11 November 2019}} The party opposes immigration and has promised to ban all immigration and refugees for two years, although Tamaki backtracked on this, saying there would not be a total ban on refugees. It also seeks to remove the right of [[New Zealand permanent residency|non-citizen permanent residents]] to vote.{{Cite web|last=Vision NZ|date=24 October 2019|title=Only NZ citizens should vote |url=https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PO1910/S00239/only-nz-citizens-should-vote.htm |access-date=24 February 2020|website=Scoop}} Vision has supported greater financial autonomy for [[Māori people]], including a Māori-owned bank and [[Ngāi Tūhoe|Tūhoe]] ownership of [[Te Urewera]].
